posts.title: Test agent-ready tools on a small website
posts.promise: Try a one-page script that lets an AI agent find and use a few site controls.
posts.whatItIs: Latch says its free, open-source script exposes search, navigation, cart, and contact-form actions to AI agents through WebMCP, a browser tool interface. A student could test a tiny version on a personal demo site, using Latch as a reference. That student project is hypothetical.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: a small business that wants its website to work with AI agents might pay for setup or monitoring; the source does not establish customer demand.
loop: Choose a test page and list the controls an agent may use.
Add a script that exposes only those controls as tools.
Ask an agent to search or navigate the test page.
Review each action and check that forms are not submitted without approval.
Record tool name and outcome locally, then inspect the results by hand.
posts.evidence: Latch's site describes a free open-source script that registers search, cart, contact-form, and navigation tools, and says it uses read-only page discovery. It describes opt-in analytics as metadata-only. Source: https://latch.tools
posts.uncertainty: The source describes Latch's product, not independent results or buyer demand. A student build would need to limit available actions and require a person to review purchases and form submissions; browser support for WebMCP may vary.
first24Hours: Make a demo page with a search box and a navigation link.
Read the Latch guide and identify which actions are safe to test.
Try one agent search and manually verify the page and resulting action.

ease.reason: A beginner can start on a demo page; adding a script and testing agent actions still requires basic web skills.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: a small business might pay for setup or monitoring, but the source gives no evidence of buyers or demand.

feasibility.reason: A limited test of search and navigation fits a four-week project; broader site actions and browser support add uncertainty.

autonomy.reason: The described script registers repeatable page actions, while a person must set boundaries and review consequential form or cart actions.

evidence.reason: The first-party site describes a working live demo and the script's actions, but supplies no independent use evidence here.

posts.title: Try a human-reviewed meeting notes loop
posts.promise: Prototype a flow that turns a meeting recording into notes and reminder suggestions.
posts.whatItIs: The sideOS site describes offering to record after a meeting window opens, transcribing on-device, writing a summary, and extracting action items. A student could prototype a flow that drafts notes and reminder suggestions from a recording they have permission to use. This adaptation is hypothetical.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: a person or small team that wants help turning meetings into follow-ups might pay; the source does not establish demand or customers.
loop: Choose a meeting recording that participants have agreed may be used.
Transcribe it with an on-device tool.
Draft a summary and a list of possible action items.
Have a person correct names, decisions, and deadlines.
Create reminders only after the person approves each one.
posts.evidence: The sideOS site says it offers one-tap recording after a meeting window opens, on-device transcription, summaries, and action items that can become reminders. Source: https://sideos.ai
posts.uncertainty: The page is a product description, not independent proof of transcription accuracy or user demand. Meeting participants must consent; a person should check the transcript and approve every reminder. This student workflow is not established as a sideOS feature.
first24Hours: Write down a consent checklist for a test recording.
Use a short recording with permission and produce a draft transcript.
Manually compare a summary and action list with the recording.

ease.reason: A small prototype can use a permitted short recording, but transcription and careful review require setup and time.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: people or small teams may pay for meeting follow-up help; the source establishes no demand or paying customer.

feasibility.reason: A draft transcript and summary are a plausible four-week experiment, with consent and accuracy checks as real constraints.

autonomy.reason: The described product automates recording support, transcription, and draft action extraction; consent and review remain human tasks.

evidence.reason: The first-party page gives a concrete meeting workflow and product demonstration, but no independent real-use evidence.

posts.title: Test a self-hosted media library idea
posts.promise: Explore whether creators want to keep media on hardware they control.
posts.whatItIs: Shotstash's repository describes it as a self-hosted media cloud for creators. A student could interview a few creators and sketch a small, local media-library workflow without claiming that Shotstash provides any specific organizing or AI feature. This proposed experiment is hypothetical.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: creators who want media hosted on their own hardware might pay for a setup or support service; the source does not show that they will.
loop: Ask a creator what media they keep and where they store it.
Record only the storage needs they choose to share.
Sketch a simple library workflow for files on hardware they control.
Have the creator review whether the sketch matches their needs.
Do not move or upload any files without explicit permission.
posts.evidence: The GitHub repository identifies Shotstash as a self-hosted media cloud for creators. Its repository page also shows an MIT license. Source: https://github.com/Aldyernesto/shotstash
posts.uncertainty: The attached source excerpt establishes the project's description but not its detailed features, working behavior, or creator demand. The proposed interview and sketch are hypothetical; a person must control any file access or hosting decisions.
first24Hours: Read the repository description and note what it does and does not establish.
Draft five neutral questions about creators' media storage needs.
Ask one creator for an interview, without requesting access to files.

ease.reason: A beginner can start with interviews and a sketch, but the source gives too little detail to build against specific features.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: creators might pay for setup or support, but neither a buyer nor a concrete purchasing need is evidenced.

feasibility.reason: Interviews and a workflow sketch fit four weeks; implementing a useful product cannot be scoped from this brief source excerpt.

autonomy.reason: The attached description does not establish an automatable loop; the proposed discovery and review work is manual.

evidence.reason: The repository establishes a named project and its self-hosted media-cloud purpose, but the excerpt provides no working demonstration details.
